Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
We will first identify the structure forced by the intersection condition, then turn the problem into an ordering problem.

---

## 1. The structure of the sets

Taking \(i=j\) gives

\[
|A_i|=i.
\]

If \(i\mid j\), then

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)=i=|A_i|,
\]

so

\[
A_i\subseteq A_j.
\]

Now for any \(i,j\), let \(g=\gcd(i,j)\). Since \(g\mid i\) and \(g\mid j\), we have \(A_g\subseteq A_i\cap A_j\). But

\[
|A_g|=g=|A_i\cap A_j|,
\]

hence

\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]

Now fix an element \(x\) that appears in at least one of the sets \(A_i\). Define

\[
S_x=\{i: x\in A_i\}.
\]

If \(i\in S_x\) and \(i\mid j\), then \(A_i\subseteq A_j\), so \(j\in S_x\). Thus \(S_x\) is upward closed under divisibility.

Also, if \(i,j\in S_x\), then \(x\in A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}\), so \(\gcd(i,j)\in S_x\). Thus \(S_x\) is closed under taking gcds.

Let \(m\) be the smallest positive integer in \(S_x\). For any \(n\in S_x\),

\[
\gcd(n,m)\in S_x,
\]

and by minimality of \(m\), we must have \(\gcd(n,m)=m\). Hence \(m\mid n\). Conversely, if \(m\mid n\), upward closure gives \(n\in S_x\). Therefore

\[
S_x=\{n: m\mid n\}.
\]

So every element belongs exactly to those sets \(A_n\) whose index is a multiple of a unique positive integer \(m\).

Let \(B_m\) be the set of elements that belong exactly to the sets \(A_n\) with \(m\mid n\). Then

\[
A_n=\bigcup_{m\mid n} B_m.
\]

Taking sizes,

\[
|A_n|=\sum_{m\mid n}|B_m|=n.
\]

Let \(b_m=|B_m|\). Then

\[
\sum_{m\mid n} b_m=n
\]

for every \(n\). By Möbius inversion,

\[
b_m=\varphi(m).
\]

Thus there are exactly \(\varphi(m)\) elements in \(B_m\).

So, up to renaming the elements, the whole construction is forced:

\[
A_n=\bigcup_{m\mid n} B_m,\qquad |B_m|=\varphi(m).
\]

---

## 2. Reducing to an ordering problem

Only the divisors of \(250\) matter:

\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250.
\]

For \(d\mid 250\),

\[
A_d=\bigcup_{m\mid d} B_m.
\]

Elements from blocks \(B_m\) with \(m\nmid 250\) appear in none of the sets \(A_d\) with \(d\mid 250\), so they do not affect the desired sum. We may label the \(250\) elements of \(A_{250}\) with \(1,2,\dots,250\), and label all other elements with larger positive integers.

We may also assume that whenever \(m\mid n\), every label in \(B_m\) is smaller than every label in \(B_n\). Indeed, suppose \(m\mid n\), but an element \(x\in B_n\) has a smaller label than an element \(y\in B_m\). Swapping the labels of \(x\) and \(y\) does not increase any \(\max A_d\):

- if \(n\mid d\), then \(m\mid d\), so both elements are in \(A_d\), and the maximum label among them is unchanged;
- if \(m\mid d\) but \(n\nmid d\), then only \(y\) is in \(A_d\), and its label decreases;
- otherwise, neither is in \(A_d\).

Thus we may assume the blocks respect divisibility.

Now for \(m\mid 250\), let

\[
C_m=\max B_m.
\]

Because all proper divisor blocks of \(m\) come before \(B_m\), we have

\[
\max A_m=C_m.
\]

Therefore the desired sum is

\[
\sum_{m\mid 250} C_m.
\]

Now consider the blocks ordered by increasing \(C_m\). Since \(m\mid n\Rightarrow C_m<C_n\), this is a linear extension of divisibility. If the first \(r\) blocks in this order have sizes \(p_1,\dots,p_r\), then all their elements have labels at most the completion time of the \(r\)-th block. Hence that completion time is at least \(p_1+\cdots+p_r\).

We can relabel the elements by making the blocks consecutive in exactly that order. This only decreases every \(C_m\). Therefore an optimal labeling may be assumed to have contiguous blocks, ordered as a linear extension of divisibility.

So the problem becomes:

> Order the eight blocks \(B_m\) for \(m\mid 250\), respecting \(m\mid n\Rightarrow B_m\) before \(B_n\), with block sizes \(\varphi(m)\), to minimize the sum of their completion times.

The sizes are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
m & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
\varphi(m) & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 20 & 20 & 100 & 100
\end{array}
\]

---

## 3. Finding the optimal order

Use the standard adjacent-swap argument: if two adjacent incomparable blocks have sizes \(p>q\), swapping them keeps the order valid and reduces the total completion time by \(p-q\). Thus in an optimal order, adjacent incomparable blocks cannot have decreasing sizes.

Now determine the order.

- \(1\) must be first.
- If \(2\) were not second, the block immediately before \(2\) would be incomparable with \(2\) and larger than size \(1\), impossible. So \(2\) is second.
- After \(1,2\), the only available block is \(5\), so \(5\) is third.
- If \(10\) were not fourth, the block immediately before \(10\) would have to be \(25\) or \(125\), both incomparable with \(10\) and larger than size \(4\), impossible. So \(10\) is fourth.
- After \(1,2,5,10\), the only available block is \(25\), so \(25\) is fifth.
- If \(50\) were not sixth, then \(125\) would immediately precede it. They are incomparable and \(100>20\), impossible. So \(50\) is sixth.
- Then \(125\) is seventh, and finally \(250\) is eighth.

Thus the optimal order is

\[
1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 10,\ 25,\ 50,\ 125,\ 250.
\]

The completion times are therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1&=1,\\
C_2&=1+1=2,\\
C_5&=2+4=6,\\
C_{10}&=6+4=10,\\
C_{25}&=10+20=30,\\
C_{50}&=30+20=50,\\
C_{125}&=50+100=150,\\
C_{250}&=150+100=250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
=1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

This value is achievable by labeling the blocks in the order above with consecutive positive integers, and labeling all other blocks with larger integers.

Therefore the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
